"I was thirsty, hungry, and unwashed. All of us detainees had been urinating and defecating in our underwear while we were detained. I saw Svetozar Andric for a third time at" this location. "This was a couple of days after the second visit." That's all I wanted to read out. Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what municipality is he from?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I said -- I described in private session where the facility is that we're talking about. I don't want to deal with it in public session.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I simply don't know the man. If you told me that he was from somewhere down there, I was born in Kalesija, I might perhaps believe that I know the man. But to be talking to him this way for three times makes no sense. Let me tell you, first of all, my conscience is completely clear. In my estimate, if I recall correctly, if they are from Paprace, there is one witness priest Pahomije, the president of the municipality Jankovic, where I was with them and I told the president of the municipality and asked the priest who was there that nobody should be harmed, not a hair on their head should be harmed. And I always fought for the security of all the prisoners. My Muslim colleagues can testify to that, both those who fought me. I fought them, they fought me --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I saw later on TV a man who was in charge of the special unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- allow me to finish --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- with great respect, your Muslim colleagues have stated in a statement that they gave to the OTP that you gave -- engaged in this sadistic and inhumane exchange; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I absolutely deny this. Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to admit those -- that one page, please, and the preceding page, the bottom paragraphs, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it consistent with our practice?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's been read on the record so I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that prisoners of war, over a hundred of them, 140, 150, were killed --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- detainees of Susica camp in --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You accept now that these -- that there was a massacre of between 140, 150 of the last remaining detainees at Susica camp at the end of September 1992, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you take great pains to deny that you were aware of it at the time in your statement. Let me just take you to the statement at paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 7, not only do you -- you describe -- you say that you were in Milici in September/October 1992; is that right? That's how you seek to distance yourself from this massacre at Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you are interpreting it the way it suits you. I did not say anywhere that I knew of the crime, and for your information, I found out about the crime only when President Karadzic's Defence contacted me and told me: Do you know about that crime? I said: Well, people are there alive to testify. I was surprised, simply. I didn't know about that crime. Second, you cannot put something to me that I did not say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So do you not accept that these detainees were killed? The last remaining detainees at Susica camp were killed before the camp was then closed down? You don't accept that now?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept it. I just have information from my assistants for morale, religious and legal affairs, Major Stanisic. When I returned I was in Milici first, then in Skelani. So when I came to the meeting with my assistants, he told me that the Susica camp was closed and that an exchange was carried out of prisoners of war pursuant to the approval of the chief of the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: When did this meeting take place then, this information you had from Major Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime on the 15th of September, at the collegium in the brigade, because he was in charge of prisoner exchange --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That was before the camp closed down --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- then --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- and that was before the massacre?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. The 15th of October, the 15th of October. Excuse me. The 15th of October. You said that the massacre was on the 13th -- the 30th. This happened on the 15th. So I am telling you, I swear before the Tribunal that I did not know until Mr. Sladojevic, during my preparation, told me about it. And the reason is the Vlasenica Brigade was formed that month, so I practically was not any more in charge of that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm aware of the time and I will be -- I would ask for another 20 minutes if possible because I have one topic I would want to deal with after Susica, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go briefly again into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- a document that I had asked to be admitted earlier was admitted marked for identification, P06456. The translation's now been uploaded so I'd ask to have that to admitted in full now, if I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the Prosecution -- the Defence's response, we'll fully admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go, please, to P03162.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from you, isn't it, that relates to operations that you were carrying out under directive 4 that, of course, you're familiar with. And let's just see what you say in this document about your activities. Just look at the second paragraph, please. And you can see there you explain that the village of Gobilje has been burnt and tomorrow the plan is to do Paljevine. This is something you report to the Drina Corps command, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This describes you burning a village in the course of operations in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that we would continue with Paljevine, is that right, and to continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And you were burning houses, weren't you, to force the Muslim population out; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not read until the end, and then we continue with Paljevine or the burning. Mr. President, I will have to explain something here in two sentences. First of all, the command of the Birac Brigade - after the 4th Armoured Brigade left, headed by Colonel Tacic - left just two active officers behind. Everything else at the command was in the military sense insufficiently trained. Those operatives who stayed in the course of the day, they had their own duty officers who would report back to the corps command with a daily report. And then in the first item you see that we had five or six casualties in the Bisina axis towards Zivinice. We had some wounded. The person who wrote that document wrote about the village of Gobilje. The village of Gobilje is to the west of the facility of Paljevine, Udrc. The village was a fortified line of defence of the Muslim forces. And then it says "and we continue on to Paljevine," not meaning to continue burning but to do facility 841, that is the facility of Paljevine where the Muslim regular forces were putting up a powerful resistance. So it was not our intention to burn any villages because it had already been destroyed in previous action by shells, but they used it as a shelter. That is for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're smiling, General. Is it amusing to you that you were burning Muslim villages during the course of these operations in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I just appear like this. I'm not smiling. Because the questions that you are putting, you are putting to a person, to a general who was not involved in things like this and would never order such a thing. Secondly, you are putting things to me that are not expert. This was not written by the commander. There was a daily report written every day to the corps command, and it would be signed by a simple warrant officer. So if you look at item 1, you will see that after five killed fighters it's not a surprise, and I even think that there was a girl who prepared this. I think that she was angry and that she said Paljevine, but I explained that that was a defence sector of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you're saying that this document describes a village as having been burned because a girl wrote it and, what, that isn't the reality, that didn't happen, this village wasn't destroyed; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Listen, again you don't understand me. Had that person been professionally trained, she would not have written it in that way. She would have written sector -- defence sector in the village of Gobilje destroyed, we continue with our action towards the Paljevine feature. A layperson would write down "we burned it," that would be a layperson. This is what I think. This is my professional opinion. As far as we're talking about Paljevine or burning, my own house was burned, my whole village --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your own house --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was burned in 1995, in June, I know -- oh, yes, yes, all right. You are not asking me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can I please --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let us see -- yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 55, line 9/10 it says [In English] "Destroyed in previous action by shells." [Interpretation] And he said "in previous fighting, the village was destroyed in previous fighting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't know what difference it make. The translator said they were -- had been already destroyed in previous action by shells. We could understand it, couldn't we?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it was fighting, not shelling of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, I said that, the sector defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, let's go to P3161, please. In the English we can see over the page, and similarly in the B/C/S, we can see again this is a report coming from the Birac Infantry Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And we can see again this is a document that is from the commander, you, of the Birac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We just look perhaps at the second page just to clarify that, in both the B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And just see ... signed by you. You'd agree? And then we --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- look at the preceding page, please. And we can see described at the bottom of the page in English --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies, it was the preceding page in English but remaining on the second page in B/C/S. I do apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So we can see in the English: "In the course of the day special units of the 1st Birac Light Infantry Brigade," and you can see where that appears in the second paragraph in the B/C/S, yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It says they took and destroyed the village of Gobilje, "thus freeing up the left flank of the main forces in the attack on Cerska. At the entry into the village, our soldiers found weapons and other military equipment as well as food and cattle which the enemy left behind when fleeing from our forces." So this is the village from which the enemy had fled which you destroyed. We see it again in this report; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The village of Gobilje had fortified positions, but between the villages of Gobilje and Paljevine there was facility 841 where there was cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you don't talk about --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they referred to that in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't talk about fortified positions here. You say that at the entry into the village our soldiers found weapons and other military equipment and then you say that had been left behind when the enemy fled. You didn't need to burn the village, did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village had been destroyed earlier. At the entrance to the village, the enemy did not have enough time to take their weapons from the trenches. It was a fortified position, so when they fled they practically left their weapons behind. You know, that was a fortified feature. So when we captured it, the enemy simply did not have time to take a part of their weaponry from the line. So they took some weaponry and some they did not. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we look at the last document, P05261.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercept, intercepted communication, and I want to read you from the bottom of it, Zivanovic - Gaborovic. This is an intercept dated the 8th of February, 1993, 10.45. Just look at the bottom, please. "Catch up with them and fuck their mothers now." "Understood." That's the answer. "Zivanovic: Hold tightly the positions ... are the Turks' houses burning? "Answer: They are burning, they are burning. "Zivanovic: Way to go, as many as possible." This is the strategy, isn't it, to force the Muslim population out of the Podrinje area, burning houses, and this is what you were doing, wasn't it, in your 1993 operations, destroying, burning houses to force people out; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the strategy of the Drina Corps, or rather, the Birac Brigade. I have to just say that in the period from 1941 to 1945, no Serbian man from age 18 to 65 was left. Everything was either killed or driven to Jasenovac. This agreement -- there was an agreement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, you spoke a bit too fast for the interpreters to understand. I'm not sure if you are responding to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the translation it was not said that he spoke fast but not enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Andric, what happened in 1941 to 1945 are not relevant. Please, shall we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just want to look at one final document, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to say that this was not the strategy of the Drina Corps or of the Supreme Command or of the Main Staff. Quite the contrary. As far as municipality of Birac is concerned, the SAO Birac government agreed with the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- municipalities of Tuzla, Kalesija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we heard that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that the population should move out safely. So there was no strategy of burning in order to do it that way; the people had already left. As for the burning and the shelling and destruction through that that happened, these were combat positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just ask you to look at one more document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: There was a huge international outcry, wasn't there, as a result of these operations in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993. I don't know in what context.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you talked about it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I said that the Security Council, I think in April, adopted Resolution 819 about the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa, if that's what you're thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to read from the report that was written at the time by the Special Rapporteur of the Commission of Human Rights. This is the front page, it's dated May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And if we could turn, please, in the English to page 5, and similarly in the B/C/S at page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm just going to read paragraphs 13 and also 15. Para 13: "The pattern of the previous seven months was changed when Serb forces reportedly went on the offensive against the Cerska enclave from 15 January 1993 until the last village, Konjevic Polje, fell on or around 10 March 1993. One hamlet was taken at a time. Every day there were thousands of shells from the tanks in the surrounding hills. In hamlets such as Gobilje, it is alleged that each house was individually targeted and people moved from house to house as the shelling progressed. Government forces would purportedly fall back to the next village, moving civilians back as they did so until that village was about to fall, too. Many of the witnesses had fled their homes with Serb forces right behind them. People who were unable to move, such as old people, invalids and the wounded, reportedly remained in the villages to be taken." And just at paragraph 15 --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we move a little bit the text -- okay. All right, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And paragraph 15, we're going to have to go over in the B/C/S, please. I'm just going to read out the B/C/S related to Cerska village and in the English which is the last couple of sentences. "One witness reports watching from the mountain above as Serb forces entered Cerska village with infantry, then tanks and then armoured vehicles: 'The houses had already been destroyed by shelling, but even if a piece of a roof was intact, the Serbs would set it on fire so that everyone else could see.'"

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: That reflects the strategy, doesn't it, destroy the villages to drive the Muslims out, burn as many houses as possible? You would accept that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I repeat that that was not our strategy and I will prove it as follows. From the Cerska area, thousands of people were moving from villages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch all the villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By taking Cerska, by capturing Cerska on the 1st of March and then Konjic on the 15th of March, Mr. President, President Karadzic actually helped together with the military leadership, with the assistance of General Morillon, to prevent revenge from the Serbian population that was returning to their villages, and it was not our goal to burn villages so that they could leave. They had already left, but we practically saved them precisely thanks to the help by the president, President Karadzic, and General Morillon. As for the Serbian villages around Srebrenica, does anybody ask why they were torched? Somebody should ask that of me. But I guarantee it was not our strategy and the military and political leadership did a great thing by preventing revenge from the Serbian people who had suffered major, major casualties in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded a whole part of the answer where the general, General Andric, talks about how many Serbs were killed before Cerska fell in the neighbouring villages. This is page 61, lines 24 and 25, nothing of that was recorded. And that is actually the pretext for the revenges that we're talking about. Could he please be asked what he was thinking of, how many of them died and by whose hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not relevant. Shall we continue. You can take up that issue in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like to admit just that portion of the report to which I've referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I think again since it's been read in, it can be sufficient. But this is based on a lot of unidentified hearsay and I don't believe it's sufficiently reliable to be admitted on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the points you raised go to the weight in the view of the Chamber. What page are you tendering, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's page 5, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit page 1 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, and the corresponding B/C/S pages, that would include page 6, I'm told. Shall we assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6460, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us why that part of Podrinje was liberated only in spring 1993, a year into the war? What was the life like in Podrinje during that year?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in 1993 we decided to launch that operation because in 1992 -- enabled all those who wanted to live together with us to remain living with the Serbs; however, the Muslims from Vlasenica, Kamenica, Zvornik went to Cerska. They set up their units there. They linked up with the units of the 28th Division led by Naser Oric and they continued to launch attacks against the positions of the Serb soldiers, i.e., the Serb villages. Even after the international community proclaimed Srebrenica, Zepa protected areas, in the depth of municipality of Milici there was a village of Visnjica and that was in 1995 and that was the introduction and all those operations. There was also Kotolac [phoen] on the Drina River as well as Rijeka river. In the depth Naser Oric's forces carried out operations in protected areas and they killed innocent people, they burned villages. They killed and they plundered as much as they could. They forced people to jump into the Drina River in order to save themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not finish your answer a while ago, i.e., your answer was not fully recorded. Before the liberation of Cerska, how many Serbian casualties were there which may have led to retaliation?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, up to then there were about 2.000 Serbian casualties. In late 1995, 3.240 according to what I remember. Mr. President, let me remind you of the 12th of March, 1992. I was a major in Bratunac when I first buried 95 Serb casualties, mostly civilians. Unfortunately, among those civilians, there were also four pregnant women. The temperature was in the 40s and Bishop Vasilije held a speech. Mrs. Biljana Plavsic was also there and they forced me to say something as well. I did say something as the commander. I don't know what I said at the time. However, among those numerous victims there were civilians and that gave me such a fright. I was so stressed that I couldn't believe that a human mind could do something like that. I turned completely grey. Kravica and Bozici in 1992, I have a list of the 38 people who were killed there, mostly elderly people and women, and a series of other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- places in the territory of Birac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't ask about Bratunac or any of these locations. These questions don't arise out of any questions that I put in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, it goes too far. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at P6460. That was the last document that we had on the screen. I'm interested in page 2. It would be page 5 in the Serbian, page 5. Page 5, paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain, regardless of the gravity and value of this exhibit, it says here government forces would allegedly withdraw to the following villages, and they would take civilians with them. Until the moment that village faced the fall too. Could you please tell us who was it who took away the civilians or who chased them away; and what does it mean when it says the government forces in the villages?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government forces were actually local communes; however, according to what I know, the units that were in Cerska and Srebrenica together with the units in Cerska ordered the civilian population to leave and go to the municipality of Srebrenica. 150 villages were destroyed around Srebrenica. They were ordered to settle in Srebrenica which was completely clean. So there were no government members, there were only commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of those government forces, i.e., the units that fought in those villages?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Muslim units which means that they were in the villages, although in the territory of Cerska there were a lot of Serbian villages. And when we liberated Cerska, like I've already told the Trial Chamber, owing to you and the military command, we forbade retaliation, we forbade anybody from entering those villages until we placed the whole territory under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What did you discover there? Were there any excavations of mass graves when those areas were liberated? Did General Morillon participate in all that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I had two conversations with General Morillon in Mali Zvornik. I remember the conversation that we had about the desire of the Muslim population from Srebrenica to move out. We --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- organised ourselves on the Tuzla-Zvornik axis and I can't remember any of the things that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I allowed some of this to go, but I think again it's straying into areas well beyond what was asked in cross-examination so it doesn't arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the issues of Cerska does arise from the document, the Mazowiecki document that she showed and the questions she asked, but it seemed like the witness had completed his answer so perhaps we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. And now can we look at P6450. I'm interested in page 4 in that document -- no. P6450. It seems that we are the cause of the confusion. I apologise. Can we now look at P3161.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did these fighters die? In this document you say that you had six fighters who were killed, among them three had their throats slit in a dugout. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that happened in the area -- let me just see, six killed. Yes. That was in the area of the Kladanj and Vlasenica -- in Bisina area. They were killed by the enemy fire, mortar fire, rifle grenades, cannons. A lot of the weaponry remained there from the 15th of May, 1992, when unfortunately that column was burnt in Tuzla, in the depots of the TO unfortunately. 1995, in an attack against the Vis feature, the SFOR forces participated in that attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, yes. Tell us, please, the three whose throats were cut, should they have been taken prisoner first? Could their throats be slit from afar?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as they took up their positions, they were arrested and their throats were slit immediately. Those fighters did not spend any time as prisoners, they were killed immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When we -- when it comes to Gobilje, when you look at the second paragraph, it says that they took and destroyed the village of Gobilje, and thus they dealt with the left flank of the main forces. What does that mean, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, Gobilje was a fortified position of the Muslim fighters and we dealt with the left flank with our brigade between the Vlasenica and Birac Brigades. They kept on coming from that sector and entering Serbian villages where they burnt and killed civilians, and then they would return to their own sector. That's how we linked up our forces and we prevented further killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in the following paragraph it says the Zvornik -- if the Zvornik Brigade continues the attack, Udrc will not be a threat to any unit. What is Udrc, was that militarily justified?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Udrc was the largest feature in the territory of Cerska. Everything that happened, all the evil that befell us started from the Udrc facility. If the Zvornik Brigade managed to conquer that facility and take it, then those operations coming from that area would stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the military standpoint, how would you qualify this?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be taking up military position, a military feature. It was not a village, it was not any such thing. In simple terms, it was a facility or a feature that was of some significance for preventing further enemy activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 -- or rather, P648 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: P6458.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 you explained -- or rather, in your statement, paragraph 8, you explained reasons for operations against the Muslim 8th OG.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 or page 4 in this document. Page 4 in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have already talked about that. I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please start reading from: "We shouldn't forget ..." You are reporting about the event that happened on the 26th of September, 1992, in Podravanje village; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us what happened there and whether that resulted in the mass burial in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th, in the village of Podravanje in Milici municipality, there was a massacre, and on the 26th that repeated in Vlasenica. Within the space of two days, 34 plus 29 people were killed, a total of 59 or 63, if my calculation is correct, and over 50 were wounded and eight people went missing --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- over the space of two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think going into this level of detail just isn't relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And unnecessary. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following page, please. And while we are waiting, I have to explain why the General spoke about Paljevine. The word "Paljevine" in our language means to burn something. However, Paljevine is a hill --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a feature. It's a trig point and its number is 841. I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, can you look here where it says that on the 2nd of March, 1993, our forces broke up resistance in the enemy stronghold in the village of Gobilje. And on the -- from that day on, that village was under our control. Was that a village, actually? What kind of resistance did the villagers of that village put up? To what degree was that village militarised?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can tell from the document that attacks were launched from that village. It was a fortified position of the enemy forces as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the take-over of command, i.e., when you became the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D9319. This is Radenko Jovicic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the statement to us. We received that from you and it was signed in 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D9319 provided the courtesy of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Just to clarify, this is the document that was handed to me during my questioning of the witness. We'd need some clarification of where it is from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where is this from --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I apologise, the witness walked up to the Defence and gave it to them during the break. So that's the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- in which this document was obtained by the Defence today. It was given to them in the break by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but the document was the one that I sent in in 2002 to the office of The Hague Tribunal in the Ramici case in Republika Srpska. utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I think this needs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree that you handed over that document to the Defence during the break? Mr. Robinson, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you object to the Defence using this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I don't, but I would like greater clarity as to the source of it because it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: -- it hasn't been accurately stated, I don't think, by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, could you lead the witness in that regard. Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are inclined to do so. I was thinking about finishing in some ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you tell us briefly what the document is. If you provided it, then probably the Prosecution have it. We will have an ERN number. So what's the document? Who was it issued by?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a document issued by the assistant for the Chief of Staff for organisation and mobilisation issues. On the stated day, in the corridor, outside of the corps command --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Go slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "On the mentioned day in the corridor outside the corps command, it was ordered that all the officers of the corps command be lined up. Let me note that no order was being read at the time or a decree on the mentioned appointments. I am not aware at all of the time when he took up the duty of the chief of corps. "On the same date, 13 July 1995, the then or the hitherto commander of the corps, General Zivanovic, came to my office and ordered that I should send out a dispatch informing all corps units that the duty of the corps commander was taken up by Major-General Milorad Radislav Krstic and that the hitherto commander, Major-General Milenko Zivanovic, was appointed to a new duty in the VJ-VRS. utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was our understanding correct that the camp was established in April as a reception centre, which held both Muslim and Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]

utterances.text: Do you know when it was that prisoners of war arrived in Susica for the first time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]

utterances.text: Were civilians within the jurisdiction of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]

utterances.text: Do you remember if Serbs and Muslims were held in that same gym or is there several rooms there?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]

In the meantime, on the border with Kladanj the civilians had already gone and Serbs came this way from the central prison in Tuzla. That's as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To what extent is the information about personal hygiene correct? Let me not repeat them.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't remember. I never set foot to Susica camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm talking about the Vlasenica gym.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- especially the gym itself, it was very clean. It had its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- auxiliary rooms. It was a sports gym where children --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's just a location which I had dealt with in private session very specifically, just so the parties are aware that that location shouldn't be identified publicly. utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before we get started with Dr. Dunjic, I just wanted to make a request that two exhibits be withdrawn which are duplicates and that's D3812 and D3815. They were duplicates of D3786 and D3793.

utterances.text: Thank you. While we are dealing with administrative matters, in light of the Defence motion for clarification which was filed before the Appeals Chamber, the Chamber was wondering whether there would be any point of holding a hearing tomorrow. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, we considered that, Mr. President.
