utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to make any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll be dealing with a lot of hypotheticals. So in my view, just thinking logically as opposed to strategically, it seems that it would be better to deal with the motion when we have more concrete information. But we're ready to proceed tomorrow if you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that it has to wait the resolution by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. President, I don't know the protocol within Chambers, but if there is anything the Trial Chamber could do to encourage the fastest possible response by the Appeals Chamber, I think under the circumstances that would be best all the way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: They'd probably also be assisted by a very quick response to the motion from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at 1D25180 in e-court, please. 1D25180. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you draft an expert report for this case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, pursuant to your request, I did make an expert report which consisted of analysing reports that were provided to you by the Prosecutor's office. It's a written report. This is the report, a copy of the report, that I have with me. I drafted this report in 2009, August 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I would like to ask you to look at page 4 in this document -- but actually, I would just like you to tell us briefly where and when you were born. I would like you to tell us about your education, about your CV, but I will go in order.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I was born in 19 -- on the 8th of April, 1950, in Belgrade, where I completed my elementary and high school education, also the faculty of medicine in Belgrade. At the same time, I got a job at the Institute for Forensic Medicine in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I please ask you to speak a bit more slowly so that everything can be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well. I am working at the Institute for Forensic Medicine of the medical faculty in Belgrade. I am a full-time professor there. I have been a full-time professor since 2000. In 1977, I got my master's degree. In 1980, I did my doctoral thesis, and that same year I specialised in forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you able to tell us briefly about your professional experience, which posts you held, and what it is that you did in the profession?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I am a forensic medical officer. This is often confused with a pathologist. A forensic expert is not the same as a pathologist. A forensic pathologist and a pathologist are two different specialties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the difference to us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The difference is in the following. A pathologist deals with illnesses and changes, morphological changes on the organs and the tissues in order to establish the type of illness or disease. A forensic pathologist on top of that deals with wounds, injuries, and all forms of violent or natural health damages in order to establish the cause of death. Therefore, the main difference lies in the fact that through the morphological and pathological substrate we determine the cause of death of a person. In the briefest possible terms, from the very beginning of my work as a doctor, I decided to specialise in forensic medicine and I worked on all forms of natural and violent deaths, which I had the opportunity to encounter during my work at the institute. Outside of the institute, in my work in the field, I was working on exhumations, on different cases. Among other things, I worked on an exhumation in 2000 because at that time I was already a director of the Institute for Forensic Medicine, so I worked on the exhumations in Batajnica about this Tribunal and Madam Carla del Ponte were personally informed about. We informed them about the way in which we worked and our objectivity. What I believed to be my moral duty is to inform you that the Institute for Forensic Medicine where I come from is one of the oldest forensic medicine schools in the area of the Balkans which started its work in the mid-19th century when we already had our own professors which were educated in the Austro-Hungarian Empire and in Czechoslovakia. So that the foundations of forensic medicines as it is practiced in our institute is based on the best forensic medical schools, this is the German school, and then over the past few decades we have enriched it with new developments that come from the Anglo-Saxon systems. In our institute, our medical students which graduate in forensic medicine study from textbooks written by our professors, but they are also presented with all other textbooks adapted from different schools, either from the Anglo-Saxon or the Russian traditions. I emphasise this because in my works up to now and in my testimony before this Tribunal up to now, I had the opportunity to see how my colleagues performed autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you please tell us how many scientific and expert works did you publish, you yourself or together with your associates?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Throughout this period, after my doctorate, after my master's degree, I published, I think, some 200 professional and scientific works. However, I would like to single out, out of all of those papers, my professional work primarily as a forensic medical expert in a project from 1995 or 1996 completed in 2000, financed by the republican government or the education ministry. This is a project involving work to establish psychosomatic consequences of torture of prisoners during the Yugoslav civil war which were held in prisoner-of-war camps by the Muslims and Muslims and Croats together as well as the Croat armed forces. That part of my research was summarised in a book and it's substantiated with photographs and documents. That book drafted by myself and my associates was presented to Madam Carla del Ponte and the book details the torture of prisoners in different camps in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. Another thing which I believe is significant is that for the past 30 years, I worked on countless number, if I can put it that way, of reports on all types of murders, deaths caused by fire-arms, other kinds of weapons, other kinds of violent deaths. One of the most significant works and reports was one done at the request of the special prosecutor and the special court in Belgrade dealing with the killing of the Serbian Prime Minister, Zoran Djindjic. This was in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: All right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I actually wanted to ask you: How frequently and how many times did you appear before courts and which ones?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I appeared before all courts in the country, the former Yugoslavia, and then in Serbia and Montenegro. But what I believe is also important to say is that in 2011, I was elected into the medical academy, the academy of sciences, on which occasion I presented my work on the killing of King Aleksandar Karadjordjevic in Marseilles and I discovered something which was not known until then, and that is that he was shot with three projectiles and it's possible that there were also four, which indicates that perhaps more than one assassin was involved. So I believe that in this area I am quite well informed. As for the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague, I already wrote that as well, I was involved in work on all of the cases so I'm going to remind myself by going through the text. So the Dusko Tadic case, the Foca case, IT-96/93; Zoran Vukovic who was charged here, I reviewed that twice, this is case IT-96-93/1; then Milan Simic, I also reviewed that documentation, this is IT-95-9 IT; I also worked on the -- I was an expert witness on the case of General Stanislav Galic, IT-98-29, where I worked on the sniper action in Sarajevo, on that topic; then I worked for the Defence in the Plavsic/Krajisnik case, this is IT-00-39 and -40; and I drafted a large report, or rather, several reports which I was not called upon to defend for whatever reasons, I mean they were not presented before the Tribunal. I worked on the Vujadin Popovic case, I mentioned that also, IT-05-88. I assisted, or rather, I was an expert witness in some way in the case against Haradinaj, testifying to the events in Kosovo in 1998; and in the case of Racak, I testified for the Prosecution on that topic here. I was a witness in the Milutinovic et al. case, IT-05-87, as well as in the Vlastimir Djordjevic case which was sometime in April 2009. And now I am testifying in this case, your case, where, other than all the documents that you provided to me on CD, DVD, and in written form, in 2011, we had the opportunity to meet when we were hearing the Prosecution expert witnesses. This is it as far as my work is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. How many documents did you receive in terms of the number of documents or the number of pages?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Believe me, this is still a mystery for me. In your case alone I received ten DVDs, I don't know how many CDs, perhaps two; and then subsequently more CDs were submitted, so we're talking about a huge number of cases, a huge body of information in electronic form. All those are collective and individual reports, autopsy reports, photos, anthropological reports, documents regarding anthropological analysis, photos from various sites, photos from post-mortems, photos of artefacts, letters that are about all the investigations that were carried out in Srebrenica. So it's really impossible for me to tell you how many pages we're talking about. I believe that you and the Trial Chamber know best how many pages those are because you have to read all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You worked on documents, right? In your profession, is it possible to work only on documents? What kind of documents do these have to be? In repeated expert analysis, should the conclusions be the same based on documents?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Working on documents alone is not an unusual procedure for an expert in forensic medicine. I as an expert in forensic medicine have to first look at a document to see whether they are adequate and whether they meet certain standards, whether they were drafted in a standard way, whether the description is good; and only after that, once I become familiar with those facts, can I then decide whether the documents are valid or not. This is how things are done. Let me paraphrase what I've just said. For example, I had a written document on the examination of the body of King Aleksandar Karadjordjevic. Two doctors described the wounds on his body. In order to check the description of the wounds, in order to arrive at the same conclusion as anybody else who after so many years, after 70 years, decided to analyse the body, you have to have an unambiguous description of the wounds following the standards of the forensic medicine. Since the description was not accurate and it was not clear whether we're talking about two gun-shot wounds or one gun-shot wound and two entry/exit wounds since that was not known, and I question the number of lesions, I was allowed to examine the clothes that were on King Aleksandar's body at the moment when he was shot. I identified a damage on the clothes that corresponded to the description. So indirectly I could accept those as the description of entry/exit wounds. In other words, documents that you delivered to me, all the documents, I had to first evaluate them in terms of their reliability, which means whether the forensic standards have been complied with, whether the documents contained all the relevant indicators. If all those existed, then either I today or somebody in 20 years' time, when we look at that same document, we will definitely arrive at the same conclusion. If I cannot arrive at that conclusion today, that means that the document in question, i.e., the description in the document is not accurate or good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the hierarchy of importance in those documents? How important is a description with regard to the final opinion of the expert?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: What is most important in any document in addition to its validity, i.e., that it has undergone an administrative procedure, which is what is done, there has to be a formal protocol applied. We are talking about the post-mortem or autopsy report. In other words, there is a standardised form of such a report which contains or has to contain certain information. What one observes during an autopsy or during an examination has to be described in detail. This is the autopsy findings. Based on the findings, we can arrive at a conclusion. For example, if there is a fracture of the femur, you have to find that in the conclusion. And then the opinion which is given at the end is arbitrary. It is based on the conclusion and on the findings; however, it is individual and it is characteristic of any one individual or expert who provides such an opinion. It's based on the know-how and the experience of such an individual. So such opinions can be very arbitrary, even incorrect. They can be malicious, they can be intentionally incorrect, and that's how we perceive them in forensic medicine. The most important thing about any document is its authenticity and precision in description, I'm talking about autopsy reports here. They have to respect a certain form so that everybody who reads this document may arrive at the same conclusion. As a result of that, opinions of various experts cannot be drastically different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Chapter 1, pages 9 through 12, you list all the documents that have been submitted to you, i.e., all those documents that you perused in order to draft your expert report. However, since we're talking about your expert report in the case of the assassination of King Aleksandar which happened in 1934, you were provided with documents and with the king's clothes. In this case, were you provided with both documents and the clothes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, in this case I was provided only with written documents in electronic form and some hard copies, and among those electronic records I found photos, black-and-white photos and coloured photos, and there were also some audio recordings that were recorded during the exhumations. I had a major problem and a major difficulty, I have to admit that, to look at a locality or a mass grave, if you will, and to find the original report as to how things were found in archaeological terms and then to find the records on how the exhumation was carried out and what were the characteristics of the grave. I had difficulty to find how bodies were removed from those pits. And then I had to go through all the files in order to find the autopsy reports for the bodies that were found at that particular locality, and then I had to go to another file in order to find the artefacts that were found in situ and yet another file where I could find the artefacts that were found on the body and yet another file where I could find anthropological reports and photos of post-mortems. The material was so ample, so extensive, that it took me a lot of time to go through all of it. I managed to cover just a few cases, a small number of locations, that is, in somewhat greater detail within the space of time that I was given for the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to the physical evidence, the biological material, the clothes, did you look for all that? Do you know whether they exist? And if you had them, would that have helped you in arriving at your findings that would be beneficial from the judiciary point of view?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: What one can see is this: Artefacts and objects that were found during exhumations and post-mortems have all been described. Their descriptions are in the reports. Some were even photographed. The main pathologist recorded all of them in the main report for certain locations. However, I did not have an opportunity to look at all of them, i.e., to look for them and to examine them personally. I received a letter on the 3rd of June, 2009, in the case that I was involved with and that was the Vujadin Popovic case, IT-05-88. Zoran Zivanovic, the Defence counsel for Vujadin Popovic, brought me a list of things which are in the possession of the Prosecutor, which were not submitted to the Prosecutor, and the third list of the physical evidence that was destroyed. I don't know based on everything that was here about the physical evidence. For example, clothes which is soiled or the traces of blood. I really don't know how I would be able to check whether that corresponds to the entries made in a report because they don't exist. The physical pieces do not exist. I give you a document with a description and then you either believe me or you don't believe me. I cannot give you an opportunity to see for yourself. I'm talking about the document that was given to me that I obviously commented upon. Why is this important? This is important not only for theoretical reasons but also from the aspect of the attitude towards the entire procedure when it comes to establishing the truth. If certain artefacts are either destroyed or lost or not properly described, as a professional I deem this to be showing disrespect to a profession as well as a negligent attitude towards the Court and the Tribunal. I allow myself as a professional forensic expert to say this because we are duty-bound when we carry out our analysis to also submit the physical evidence which may be of importance for the Trial Chamber and which may corroborate our claims, and the Trial Chamber must have the artefacts in its possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be customary for destroying materials before they are used by the Defence, and what is then the position of the Defence and the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of who is involved, either the Prosecutor or the Defence, it doesn't really matter. If artefacts are destroyed, neither the Prosecutor nor the Defence are able to check things. In this situation the question was raised. Somebody asked me, as a matter of fact, in the Vujadin Popovic case and somebody told me that the artefacts were photographed and described. And then I said: Well, wait. A photo cannot replace an expert report which involves description and the traces and everything else, because I don't know what's on the other side of the photo. A photo is two-dimensional. I don't know what's behind the photo. So a photo can never replace physical evidence and to be considered as unambiguous or fully reliable in our forensic profession, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us this: The presence of biological material on artefacts, can this be established from a photo? Can it be established in any other way by a direct inspection of such artefacts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Only by a direct inspection. A photo will, for example, indicate that there was a projectile and that there are projectile -- there are traces on the projectile. You cannot tell whether those are the traces of blood or rust or any other such thing that may exist. A photo cannot tell you that. In order to be able to establish that, I have to carry out a full analysis and this applies to every forensic expert. Once I have carried out a forensic analysis, I can tell you what I found. I can apply a DNA analysis in the case of biological material, and then I can tell you who the body belonged to, i.e., whose body the projectile passed through and inflicted death on that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned three types of physical evidence, the physical evidence that was provided to the Prosecution, the evidence that was never provided, and the evidence that was destroyed. What is the ratio between the three? In your view, how much of the material was destroyed and how come that some of the items were never received by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to consult my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you're looking at, which chapter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: It's Chapter 3, page 20. Here it goes, the list of destroyed items, which is unnumbered, according to my calculation there are more than 1.300 of them. The items in this list were recovered from almost all the graves claimed to have been linked with Srebrenica. It follows from that table that a significant number of identification documents found in the graves had been destroyed -- has been destroyed. For instance, 34 IDs from the Lazete 1 grave, 34 were destroyed and three were in and out provided to the Tribunal to begin with. Shreds of fabric that were important were also destroyed because they were used as blindfolds for some of the exhumed individuals, elsewhere as ligatures, and of course they may be used for other purposes as well, we're talking about the fabric. That fabric would have special forensic significance because now, as things stand, I am not in a position to tell you, and I mean the Tribunal in general, whether what has been said about certain types of fabric in certain grave-sites is correct as to the way they were used. Was the strip of fabric truly where it is claimed that it was ligature knotted or was it a rubber band that would be used for tying up hair or as headband, et cetera. And of course, 30 to 40 similar strips of fabric can be found in one locality, and that of course might indicate or point to one answer. So this is just this one piece of information that is highly significant because it paves the way for manipulation in different directions and so on and so forth. It follows from table 1 that the entire artefacts retrieved from grave-sites, only 21.6 per cent were preserved, that 37.1 per cent were never even provided to the Tribunal and 41.29 per cent have been fully destroyed. So I'm referring to what is contained in these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition to elements of biological material present, when it comes to artefacts, clothing, personal effects, was it possible that the elements retrieved on them were of origin other than biological and which could, nevertheless, contribute to the establishment of the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In addition to the biological material, which is very important for identification purposes, such as DNA testing, there are other items, personal effects, clothing, which may be contaminated with a variety of substances, and I mean toxic substances. They can be charred or damaged through a projectile, a shell, or in some other way. All these are issues that may help and facilitate the explanation of a death. If you have a person with shrapnel injury and if you find burnt clothing and charred bones on that person, this will allow you to come to a conclusion that the individual was injured by a shell which exploded nearby, that there may have been other individuals in that same area who may have incurred similar injuries and this may allow you to conclude that the individual was killed in shelling in combat, let's say. So if all the individuals retrieved in an area had shrapnel injuries, they could all have perished from a single shell and similar. So these are the sort of forensic conclusions that may arise from the analysis of a single artefact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the absence of soft tissue, where there is full skeletonisation, can the clothing reveal the type of asset that has caused the death of an individual, whether it was a projectile, a shell, or something else? Would it be possible to establish this on the basis of clothing as you were able to do in the case of King Aleksandar? Could one arrive at certain conclusions with the help of clothing in the absence of soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: If a corpse is skeletonised with no soft tissue but there is a presence of clothes, the defects present in the clothing which need to be examined closely would, as a rule, if they were the result of a projectile or shrapnel, have to be consistent with the injuries visible on the hard tissue, of course not soft tissue because it's not there. On this basis, the degree of probability rises that this individual may have incurred a certain type of injury, if the defects present on the hard tissue and the clothing are consistent. Of course, this does not allow you to make a full assertion. It's quite a different matter if you have to find what the cause of death was. We're talking here only about identifying injuries and damage to the clothes. Now, what did I have? I only had an incomplete description of the injury to the torso and it was on the basis of the description of the clothing that I was able to tell that the description is consistent with the injury as described. However, I did not talk about the cause of death. I only said what was possibly the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 98, line 1, the Professor said that probability rises and this is not what is recorded. So probability rises if we have clothing. Is that the case, Professor, probability increases?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was supposed to take care of artefacts, clothing, personal effects? Who was supposed to have custody over these matters and to provide them to the parties to a proceeding?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I can only assume what the case was based on what the practice is in our jurisdiction. It is all up to the court. The court will decide what sort of evidence will be kept in the court records and they can be made available to the parties to the proceeding. I don't know what sort of system was applied at the site itself. I suppose that the pathologist in charge or the investigator in charge of a certain site would be the one to say which bodies would be placed in a refrigerator unit, which bodies would be sent for autopsy once exhumed, what sort of item would be kept where. So I suppose that it would be either the investigator in charge of a locality or the pathologist in charge. The pathologist in charge who, in my view, were the forensics Mr. Lawrence and Patrick --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- had to take care of that because I've just indicated what the importance of these artefacts can be later at trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have one name missing, Clark?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and Christopher Hamilton Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they were well aware of it, just as you are; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: What I said was that they too are aware of all these issues that I've mentioned, and I do believe that what was done was outside of their knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see a document whereby the Tribunal or the Prosecutor's office, which was in possession of these artefacts, provided their approval that such a large number of artefacts be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any such document. I don't know who issued the order to destroy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find in these descriptions that the clothing or artefacts were tested for the presence of gunpowder or other chemical substances that would in addition to biological substances help establish the cause, manner, and time of death?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall this. I think that gunpowder residue was not tested. I even think that Mr. Haglund, the archaeologist in question who, when asked by us about a certain assertion of his that I'm going to refer to later, said himself that no such tests for gunpowder residue were done. I can confirm at this time, after all that time, that any positive tests, if obtained, would not in fact have any evidentiary probative value for the Court. Even if gunpowder residue were to be found, this does not mean that the part of body or clothing tested was, in fact, in the vicinity of the barrel of a fire-arm that caused that injury. Because gunpowder residue may be transferred from one surface to another. If I have gunpowder residue on my hands and I take this note pad in my hands and put it elsewhere, the note pad will have gunpowder residue. So that much is true if the test for gunpowder is positive. If it's negative, that again doesn't mean anything because of the lapse of time. So in fact, no tests for gunpowder residue would carry any probative value for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the presence of gunpowder residue be able to, based on its pattern, indicate that it was a soldier or a civilian, or could you tell us anything about those who opened fire from a fire-arm?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Finding gunpowder residue on the palms of hands, the lower arms, or parts of clothing may indicate that the person in charge was in contact with items such as a fire-arm which, when fired, left gunpowder residue. Now, was this person a combatant in the sense of being a member of the opposing side is not something that is up to me to establish. As a forensic officer, I am there to establish whether there is any gunpowder residue, where, what is the concentration, the pattern, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the documents that you attached quite a bit of significance to and you deal with in Chapter 2 at page 12 is the document by Dusan Janc, Prosecution investigator, dated 13 March and 9 April 2009. Can you tell the parties what the gist and significance of the document are and how this document was important for you as a forensic expert?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I became familiar with the document in the Vujadin Popovic case. A report made by Investigator Dusan Janc on 13 March, a report made by that same investigator on 9 April 2009, those were the documents that you have just indicated. I have it here, a copy of it. And I referenced them here. To me as a forensic expert, the document has multi-fold significance, and I mean the report done by the ICTY Prosecution investigator. It contains a number of evidentiary materials that I had my doubts about when I was looking at the various findings. This is what it's about. He produced a report on the 13th of March which has annexes A and B, where the total number of primary and secondary graves is indicated, those primary and secondary graves that are mutually connected through DNA testing. We are talking about mass graves of sorts. Following his analysis, he said that the total number of mortal remains in primary and secondary graves hailed from mass execution sites, Orahovac, Petkovci dam, Kozluk, Pilica. The first term that is used here is "mass execution sites." As a forensic expert, my understanding of the term is as the site of execution or firing by a firing squad. In other words, it's a term which predetermines the character and type of injury present in those who were exhumed. And what is it that has been exhumed? In his corrigendum which is visible here, it is stated as follows: "This corrigendum," we're talking about the second or third paragraph, "is submitted in order to clarify and correct the facts regarding Kravica and Branjevo as execution sites and identified individuals connected to these execution sites as presented on pages 36 and 37 of that report." He himself goes on to say: "Regarding the Kravica execution site, not all of the currently identified individuals (total of 1319) can be attributed to this execution site. This conclusion is based on different sources ..." And then he goes on to list the sources. They include expert reports, documents, witness statements and their testimonies. And then he goes on to say: 12 of the individuals found in grave Glogova 1 have to be excluded in relation to Kravica because they are victims who returned from Serbia to the Army of Republika Srpska and then they disappeared and were shot sometime in July -- 26 of July of 1995. Then bodies of individuals from locations other than the Kravica warehouse and the second piece of evidence is the bodies of persons from locations other than the Kravica warehouse which were also taken to the Glogova -- he himself says from the Vuk Karadzic school, in Bratunac, up to 80 bodies. According to the testimonies of protected witnesses, then from Potocari, 6 to 7; Konjevic Polje, 10 to 15; and along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, one full truck of collected bodies. From what he has written, it does not only arise that the bodies linked to Kravica is not the number of bodies that was identified, that those are bodies that were found that were subsequently brought, but you can see that these were bodies from the wider area, not only from Srebrenica but from the broader area and that they were buried. So now we have the question -- since the identifications were carried out there, I'm going to link that and then I will come back to this later. This means the following for a forensics expert, that in the Glogova site there were subsequent burials carried out, that bodies were brought that has already decomposed, which means that if the bodies were already decomposed, it means that the death occurred much earlier, before July 1995. And from Janc's report, his first report, it can be seen from the list of victims linked to Srebrenica includes all of these cases related to Kravica, includes the cases from Potocari, 1 to 7, 1 and 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Potocari 1 and 2 and Tisova 7 even cases are included from Bljeceva which the cantonal prosecutor's office in Tuzla declared, for these 46 victims, had nothing to do with Srebrenica. This is on page 14 of my report. Therefore, the Janc report has to be interpreted - and I am interpreting it from the forensic aspect - as practically confirming my view from previous analysed autopsy reports and previous cases where I asserted that if exhumed bodies in one location which have different degrees of putrification, that could indicate that there is a different time of death, one; different time of burial under 2; different causes of decomposition, and not just that a different degree of putrefaction would reflect the actual situation in the grave as Mr. Lawrence wrote. And even the archaeologist Richard Wright when I listened to him. Why do I say this? I say it because when I -- actually, when Mr. Christopher Lawrence was asked if different degrees of putrefaction can indicate different time of death, he answered yes, here before this Tribunal when I was just a consultant and when I was listening to his testimony as requested by the Prosecution in 2011. You will recall that. Therefore, the report by Dusan Janc is important in several aspects because it overturns the thesis that those people on the list who are missing in connection with Srebrenica were all -- all died in Srebrenica within a ten-day period and they did not because some of them died much earlier. And I proved that in my expert report because according to documents provided by the Prosecution, this person died in 1993. This is Potocari 1 and 2. Then Bljeceva, Bljeceva 1 which was discovered, there are 46 cases there of persons buried and expected before the events in Srebrenica and the cantonal prosecutor's office in Tuzla wrote that these cases are unrelated to Srebrenica. So that somebody who wrote a report for the ICMP or any other organisation for missing persons included those cases as well. What else I would like to emphasise is this. This protected witness who was here, I don't know who it is, PW161, doesn't matter what his name is, he said that a full truck of bodies was gathered -- P, PW, P. It's not K, correct it, it's P, PW161. A full truck of collected bodies. So now I put the question where they were collected from and what was the state that these bodies were in. Because if a body, as Janc said, is found in a primary grave, Glogova 1, and a part of that same body in primary grave-site Glogova 2, then either Glogova 1 is the primary grave for that body or it's the secondary grave for that same body or, and what is more probable in my opinion, is that it's a primary grave-site for both parts of the body but who was buried because it -- the body had already -- previously had putrefied and these were two separate body parts in two different areas, so one part was buried in Glogova 1 and the other in Glogova 2, and when you do the DNA analysis, you can actually see that it is one person. When you do the DNA analysis, a certain number found in one place has to be connected. You cannot count the same person as being buried in Glogova 1 and in Glogova 2. You have to subtract some numbers here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean then that the conclusion is, or rather, how does this relate to conclusions that some body was a victim of execution and then was subsequently buried in one grave and then transferred so that a part of that body was buried in a different grave? Can you make that conclusion if these options are possible or specially if one were to say that there are two primary graves and then in both primary graves there are parts of one and the same body?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I cannot accept it in that form, that it's a question of execution. The probability is very slight that something like that could happen. In my view, finding parts of a single body on two different locations would rather indicate that that particular person was either killed or died or the body putrefied, and then due to different external conditions the body parts were separated, which indicates also the role of animals. Possibly a person with an open wound would attract wild animals. And then you would have disarticulation so that parts of a body that are disarticulated would be found in different graves. This report is significant in itself because it indicates that victims were buried in several time-periods in the same place, that some were already decomposed even before they were brought, and that would indicate -- I apologise, that would indicate different times of death. That is the essence of Janc's report. And then he corrects himself. And of course something that I cannot accept is that the term "places of mass execution" is continually used. Mass execution sites would imply executions in a certain area, executions being carried out in a certain area. But based on my analysis and examination of autopsy report, there is a very small, a limited number of persons, with injuries. I couldn't even find a body that I could say was the body of a victim who was executed, except for those people where it was established beyond any doubt that there were ligatures, wires or ropes. In such cases where such ligatures were found, I would believe that they were victims of executions. There is a very slight difference with others where no ligatures were found. That doesn't mean that all those persons died by execution. There could be -- the cause of death could be shrapnel, projectiles, one or two of them which could indicate death caused by shells as a consequence of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you. Are you able to tell us how many bodies were found with ligatures who without doubt could be considered to be victims of execution? Could you please tell us how many such bodies did investigators find, bodies with ligatures?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Taking into account the descriptions and firm evidence, photographs and descriptions, you would say that some 400, 450, or 500 bodies were found with such ligatures. And as a forensic expert, I can accept only that number of persons as being victims of executions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that line 1, 107 has erroneous numbers, it's between 475.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I apologise, 400, 450, to 500. This is what Dean Manning cited. I would even cite a larger number because I did not check all the reports after 2000. So I draw the line there. So as a forensics expert, I would stand by that number. As for all the other numbers, those people who are victims of gun-shot wounds, shrapnel, blast wounds, in those cases there is nothing that would indicate executions at, as I keep repeating here, places of mass execution. I simply cannot accept that term because this did not occur in one place but there were several places and that number is incorrect. In the same way that I proved that the number linked to Kravica is incorrect and that would apply to all the other cases as well. I said here -- just one second. Let me find the place where I state that conclusion. Ah, yes. One more conclusion, if there is time, based on the Janc report. The bodies where parts of bone or fragments of bone were found which are connected by DNA to some other location, only those bodies parts are connected to that particular location. Everything else in that primary or secondary grave, irrespective of which, especially if we are talking about secondary grave-sites, are not bodies that were brought from the primary grave. There is no evidence of that, not Lawrence or Clark can prove that. Meaning, in other words, only those body parts which are connected to a primary or a secondary grave by their DNA, they can be connected to that primary or secondary grave. All the other bodies that were found there must be connected -- actually, must be considered to be buried in that primary grave. This is not a theoretical conclusion; this is a substantial conclusion, there is a secondary grave. But it is a question whether an archaeologist can tell when the secondary graveyards were created. Were they enriched subsequently? He couldn't say that but he could not rule it out either, that the secondary graves and the primary graves also had a large number of decomposed bodies buried there later, bodies that were found in the broader Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You quoted somebody as saying "enriched" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop here today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I just wanted this in line 7 what was missing, the Professor didn't say that. This was said by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Richard Wright and Hamilton Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That the graves were enriched. It is not in the transcript, but that means subsequent burial, bodies that were buried subsequently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Buried subsequently, that would be the correct term. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's there, I heard that, line 7 on this page. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to clarify if it's the Professor 's evidence that Richard Wright and Dr. Lawrence said that those graves were enriched? Is that what he's saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is my diary at the time when they testified, so I'm just going to refer you to the day and the time of day.

utterances.text: [No interpretation]
